Why restoring Chakaria Sundarbans is essential
item.description:
Chakaria Sundarbans, once a blessing for Bangladesh’s coastal environment, mainly covered parts of the Dulahazara and Badarkhali areas.

Although its destruction began with the establishment of settlements, the forest was cleared primarily to make way for shrimp farming.

The World Bank, the Asian Development Bank (ADB), the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and groups of influential local interests all contributed to its destruction in pursuit of their respective interests.

Grameen Bank, a Nobel Peace Prize-winning institution, also established an aquaculture project on 10 acres of land divided into 30 plots, which remains in operation today.

Chakaria Sundarbans was one of the oldest mangrove forests in the subcontinent. In the 1950s, it covered approximately 21,102 acres.

Subsequently, the authorities declared 18,508 acres as reserved forest and designated the remaining area as protected forest. Today, only a single sundari tree survives. On 24 July 2025, Prothom Alo published an investigative report titled “Forest with only one tree”.

The process of leasing out Chakaria Sundarbans began in 1977. In 1985, the Ershad government accelerated the forest’s destruction by introducing a shrimp farming policy.

Under this policy, the authorities could lease any forest land suitable for shrimp farming to interested parties.

Researchers believe that if Chakaria Sundarbans had remained intact, the 1991 cyclone would not have claimed the lives of hundreds of thousands of people in a single night.

Initiatives to restore the forest

On 28 March this year, Prothom Alo organised a discussion at the Chakaria upazila parishad conference room to explore ways to restore Chakaria Sundarbans.

The meeting brought together Prothom Alo Editor Matiur Rahman, forestry professors, experts, officials from relevant government departments and representatives of local civil society.

As someone who attended the discussion, I witnessed participants pledge their support for restoring the destroyed forest. Prothom Alo also published a special full-page supplement, highlighting the key points raised at the meeting.

The good news is that, according to a report published by Prothom Alo on 21 September under the headline “Hope for reviving Chakaria Sundarbans”, an NGO had planted 80,000 bain (Avicennia alba) trees across 25 acres along the Badarkhali Channel in Chakaria Sundarbans.

The survival rate of the bain trees has been encouraging. In June this year, another 40,000 bain trees were planted across a further 25 acres of the forest.

However, the ecosystem must first return to a healthy, natural state before large-scale tree planting can begin. The land must therefore be recovered before restoration efforts can proceed. For this reason, strong government intervention is particularly important.

According to Prothom Alo, Shaikh Faridul Islam, state minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change, said that although various organisations had received leases for land in the Chakaria Sundarbans area, 4,000 acres of forest land remained recorded in the name of the Forest Department. The government’s first priority is to reclaim this land.

Because the authorities have failed to demarcate land leased by the ministries responsible for fisheries, agriculture and land, leaseholders have also encroached on land belonging to the Forest Department. The government plans to cancel the other leases after reclaiming the forest land.

The question now is whether this process will fall victim to bureaucratic red tape.

Coexistence can offer a solution

Since the 1980s, Bangladesh’s shrimp industry has become part of the global supply chain. The existing global supply chain model, however, often encourages aggressive commercial practices.

Yet shrimp farming could have continued alongside the Sundarbans. Instead, Chakaria Sundarbans fell victim to the relentless pursuit of profit by those involved in the industry.

In the 1980s, shrimp ranked second only to the garment industry among Bangladesh’s export sectors. There is no doubt that the substantial profits from shrimp farming improved the financial circumstances of many people at the local level.

However, the industry has caused far more harm. Shrimp farming has contributed to numerous socioeconomic and environmental problems, including forest destruction, ecological imbalance, local disputes and conflicts, the leasing of land belonging to small-scale fish farmers, and the loss of land rights among poor local residents.

Shaikh Faridul Islam, state minister for Environment, Forest and Climate ChangeAlthough various organisations had received leases for land in the Chakaria Sundarbans area, 4,000 acres of forest land remained recorded in the name of the Forest Department. The government’s first priority is to reclaim this land.

Researchers believe these problems could have been reduced if shrimp farming had maintained ecological balance rather than destroying the entire ecosystem.

Discussions with experts and local residents at a meeting organised by Prothom Alo in Chakaria on 28 March, along with consultations with other specialists, suggest that shrimp farming and mangrove forests can coexist through a system known as “silvofishery”. However, those involved must abandon the mindset of trying to take everything for themselves.

A roundtable discussion at the Prothom Alo office on 10 September also highlighted mangrove-based shrimp farming as a potential solution. Rising temperatures caused by climate change have increased shrimp mortality under conventional farming methods to 64 per cent.

However, maintaining mangrove vegetation around shrimp enclosures can lower temperatures and reduce the mortality rate to 50 per cent. Participants said trials of this method across 100 hectares in Paikgachha, Khulna, had produced these results.

At the discussion, however, Mohammad Amir Hosain Chowdhury, chief conservator of Forests at the Forest Department, recommended implementing this mangrove-based system outside the natural mangrove forests of the Sundarbans.

In other words, the authorities should test the method at a new location rather than in areas where natural Sundarbans forests still survive.

Chakaria Sundarbans would be an ideal site for such an initiative, as we have a responsibility to make amends for the historical damage inflicted on this forest.

In his 1926 study, “The Flora of Chakaria Sundarbans”, James Cowan listed 53 plant species found in the forest. Chakaria Sundarbans once provided a habitat for tigers, deer and numerous bird species. It also served as a breeding ground for fish.

The destruction of the forest has depleted local fish stocks. Restoring the forest would help lost wildlife return, increase marine fish breeding and maintain ecological balance.

The mangroves of the Sundarbans act as a natural barrier protecting coastal areas. Understandably, the coastal areas of Chakaria and Pekua face considerable risks from cyclones and storm surges.

Researchers believe that if Chakaria Sundarbans had remained intact, the 1991 cyclone would not have claimed the lives of hundreds of thousands of people in a single night.

Local residents who attended the discussion organised by Prothom Alo in Chakaria also said that the damage would have been considerably less if the forest survived. That cyclone struck the Cox’s Bazar and Chattogram regions particularly hard.

Experts believe that restoring Chakaria Sundarbans would help reduce the speed of powerful winds and protect nearby communities from the impact of storm surges.

In its 21 September report, Prothom Alo identified four challenges to restoring Chakaria Sundarbans: leaseholders’ reluctance, disruption to tidal flows caused by embankments around polders and shrimp farms, soil degradation resulting from years of salt exposure and shrimp farming and changes to the natural flow of water.

Restoring the forest is essential for our survival

Scientists have repeatedly warned that climate change and global warming will increase the intensity and frequency of cyclones in the future. Coastal forests are therefore essential to protecting people and other living creatures.

Scientists also recommend creating new forests beyond those that already exist. Yet we continue to destroy forests one after another. Restoring Chakaria Sundarbans, which once covered an area of 30 square kilometres, is therefore essential to our survival.

Mangrove forests can absorb far more carbon dioxide than ordinary forests. At a time of rising global temperatures, Chakaria Sundarbans could help keep local temperatures at tolerable levels by absorbing carbon from the atmosphere.

According to recent research, coastal mangroves, including the Sundarbans, store at least 150 megatonnes of carbon per hectare. Based on this estimate, Chakaria Sundarbans, which covered approximately 8,498 hectares, could have stored 1,274,700 metric tonnes of carbon.

Mangrove forests serve as important carbon sinks and rank among the most effective coastal carbon ecosystems. Their destruction therefore causes two forms of harm simultaneously. When trees are cut down, the carbon they would have stored is released, compounding the damage.

Climate scientists consider diverse mangrove forests one of the key ways to strengthen resilience against the potential rise in sea levels caused by climate change. Mangroves also play a vital role in increasing land elevation through biogenic processes.

Coastal erosion, cyclones and other disasters cause extensive damage to coastal housing, fuel and sanitation systems, transport networks and infrastructure as a whole. Chakaria Sundarbans is essential to protecting these assets.

Researchers say mangrove forests reduce both the speed and the force of storm surges and strong winds. Coastal mangrove forests not only store carbon but also supply dissolved organic carbon to the sea.

Restoring the forest would provide sources of food, water, fish, grazing land for livestock, fuel, construction materials, medicines, wild foods, honey, grass and marine food resources.

These benefits would strengthen the local economy. Ecotourism could also develop around the restored forest, creating further economic opportunities.

Restoring Chakaria Sundarbans is not merely a matter of environmental activism; it is a struggle for our survival. We must learn from the extensive loss of life and property caused by the 1991 cyclone, when Chakaria Sundarbans no longer stood to protect the coast. Rebuilding this forest is essential to safeguarding the future of the next generation.

Discussions with experts and local residents at a meeting organised by Prothom Alo in Chakaria on 28 March, along with consultations with other specialists, suggest that shrimp farming and mangrove forests can coexist through a system known as “silvofishery”.

Challenges to restoring the forest

In its 21 September report, Prothom Alo identified four challenges to restoring Chakaria Sundarbans: leaseholders’ reluctance, disruption to tidal flows caused by embankments around polders and shrimp farms, soil degradation resulting from years of salt exposure and shrimp farming and changes to the natural flow of water.

However, several other challenges stand in the way of restoring Chakaria Sundarbans. One of the most significant is the international market for shrimp.

As mentioned earlier, the World Bank jointly implemented a shrimp farming project with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) in the 1980s.

The Asian Development Bank (ADB) also ran a separate project. Although the World Bank withdrew amid criticism at the time, it resumed investment in shrimp farming across 14 coastal districts in 2018 under the Sustainable Coastal and Marine Fisheries Project (The Daily Star, 14 July 2026).

Another major challenge is the extensive industrialisation of Maheshkhali Island. Many trees have already been cut during the construction of the Matarbari coal-fired power plant.

In addition, forest clearance continues to make way for the Matarbari Port Access Road. Has anyone sought expert advice on how to carry out these projects without destroying the forest?

Many countries across Asia, Africa and Latin America have successfully restored lost mangrove forests. The key condition, however, is to restore the ecosystem of the area where the forest once stood to its original state.

This allows the mangrove forest to regenerate naturally. Political will, however, remains the most critical factor in achieving this goal.

During a visit to the Chakaria area, I learnt that most people across several generations were unaware that a vast forest known as Chakaria Sundarbans had once existed there.

However, as the issue has recently attracted media attention, future generations may learn that Chakaria Sundarbans could not be restored despite the availability of solutions. And the reason is lack of political will.

item.title: US lifts sanctions on daughter of Myanmar military-linked businessman
item.description:
The United States lifted on Friday sanctions on the daughter of a Myanmar businessman accused of supporting the country's military, according to the US Treasury Department's website, after she filed a suit seeking removal from the blacklist.

The move comes after Reuters reported this week that the Trump administration had opened talks with Myanmar's military-installed government, reversing US policy that sought to isolate the generals who overthrew elected leaders in 2021.

It was unclear if the decision to remove Myanmar national Theint Win Htet from the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List (SDN List) was a result of the talks.

After the 2021 coup, former President Joe Biden's administration imposed sanctions on senior Myanmar military officers and companies it accused of providing support for the military junta, which triggered a nationwide civil war that has killed an estimated 100,000 people and displaced more than 3.5 million.

The Treasury in January 2024 targeted the Shwe Byain Phyu Group of Companies, its founder Thein Win Zaw and his family, saying the company imported and distributed petroleum on behalf of the military and that the family owned at least 20 companies closely associated with the regime.

Thein Win Zaw's adult daughter, Theint Win Htet, sued the Biden administration seeking her removal from the SDN List, but her case was dismissed in February 2025. The sanctions freeze any US assets of those targeted and generally bar Americans from dealing with them.

The US in July 2025 lifted sanctions on several other Myanmar nationals and a firm under sanctions for aiding the military.

Theint Win Htet filed a new complaint in July this year, arguing that she has no active role in her father's business affairs, adding that the sanctions had interrupted her studies in the US, where she completed a bachelor's degree at New York University and was enrolled in a master's program at Columbia University.

"Plaintiff’s US credit cards have been blocked, her foreign bank accounts have been restricted, closed, or refused, and she has been unable to complete her university studies in the United States," said the complaint by Theint Win Htet, who said in the complaint she now lives with her mother in Bangkok. Her mother was removed from the sanctions list last year.

Campaign group Justice For Myanmar denounced the US move at a time when it said the Myanmar military was escalating attacks on civilians. "It is deplorable that the US government continues to delist Myanmar cronies and their family members that provide funding for the junta's terror," the group said.

Theint Win Htet's lawyer, Washington-based sanctions specialist Erich Ferrari, filed a notice with the US District Court for the District of Columbia on Friday voluntarily dismissing the lawsuit after her delisting. Ferrari declined to comment.

item.title: Ex-BCL leader Mahfuzul Haider dies in Kolkata
item.description:
Mahfuzul Haider Chowdhury (Roton), former general secretary of now-banned Bangladesh Chhatra League, has passed away. He was 48 years old.

He died on Saturday morning while undergoing treatment at a hospital in the Kasba area of Kolkata.

Two former members of parliament from the Awami League (activities banned) confirmed that Mahfuzul Haider had long been suffering from stomach cancer.

Following the ouster of Sheikh Hasina on 5 August 2024, Mahfuzul Haider Chowdhury went to India. After his cancer diagnosis, his treatment initially began in Chennai. He was later shifted to Kolkata, where he had been undergoing treatment at Ruby General Hospital.

Mahfuzul Haider Chowdhury served as the central general secretary of the Chhatra League (now banned) from 2006 to 2011. He was an alumnus of Dhaka University.

He is survived by his wife and two children.

item.title: Two crude bombs thrown in front of Prime Minister’s Office at midnight
item.description:
Miscreants threw two crude bombs in front of the Prime Minister’s Office in Tejgaon, in the capital. One of them exploded, while the other was defused.

The incident took place at around 1:15 am on Friday night. A bomb disposal team of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) defused one of the crude bombs.

Ibne Mizan, deputy commissioner (DC) of the DMP’s Tejgaon division, told Prothom Alo on Saturday morning that two motorcyclists arrived at the scene and stayed there for two to three minutes. During that time, they surveyed the surrounding area. They then threw the two crude bombs and left.

Information suggests that the two motorcyclists headed towards Kafrul Road via Agargaon.

He added that police teams launched an operation immediately after the incident. They are collecting CCTV footage from surrounding areas to identify those involved. Police are working to arrest them.

item.title: Dhruv Rathee arrested over Jantar Mantar protest
item.description:
INDIA-POLITICS/GEN Z

Police in the Indian capital detained scores of protesters on Saturday amid patrols by thousands of security forces, with travel and telecoms links suspended, in a lockdown to stop a youth protest asking the election chief to quit.

The protest by the "Cockroach" youth movement, aims to draw thousands of demonstrators against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a revision of voter lists that critics say favours Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party.

Television images showed police in the central business district of New Delhi chasing down a few dozen young protesters, some wearing backpacks, before they were loaded into vehicles and hauled away.

About 200 protesters were detained in the area, a police source told Reuters. Those detained outside Delhi included protest supporter Dhruv Rathee, a popular figure on YouTube, a police spokesperson said.

With metro stations and markets shut and mobile internet suspended, police boarded buses to check for protesters after stopping them at points of entry into the city, with cars and other vehicles also subjected to checks, Reuters witnesses said.

Barricades and concrete blocks stopped traffic, while anti-riot vehicles mounted with tear gas guns were stationed on key routes, they said.

"Why is the prime minister so scared of the country's youth, the country's people?" Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the self-named 'Cockroach Janta Party' that called the protest, asked on Saturday, shortly before leaving for Delhi.

"Why did you need to close all the railways, the metro, the internet has been closed, roads have been closed? ... this is nothing but fear," he told the ANI news agency in the financial capital of Mumbai.

The protesters have said they plan to gather at Jantar Mantar, a protest site designated by authorities in the heart of New Delhi, at 10 a.m.

New challenge to Modi

The protest, touted by the CJP as an effort to "Save Democracy", is planned as the biggest of a series of demonstrations launched last week after the Indian Express newspaper said Kumar's deputies had queried and disagreed with him over list revisions that dropped about 130 million voters.

That number exceeds the population of Japan.

Opposition parties have long accused the government of trying to fix voter lists to its advantage and were quick to resurrect the allegations following the report.

Kumar has not commented but the Election Commission and the BJP have denied the allegations.

The BJP says Modi's popularity and India's economic growth are key reasons for its electoral dominance and accuses opposition parties of misleading the country as they are unable to win elections.

Nonetheless, the near daily protests by opposition groups pose a new political challenge to Modi, just months after similar demonstrations forced his education minister to quit over exam paper leaks.

They also come months before a series of key state elections starting in early 2027, among them one in the most populous state of Uttar Pradesh, ruled by the BJP.

On Friday, Delhi police said they had not given permission for the protest and violators would face the force of the law.

Their "temporary and precautionary" curbs aimed at regulating people's movement, preventing overcrowding, maintaining public order, and ensuring the safety of protesters and others in the affected areas, police said in a statement.

CJP leaders rejected the police decision and said they would go ahead with the protest as it was their fundamental right.

Deletions affected state polls, opposition alleges

The protesters accuse the BJP of using the revision of voter lists to sway election results, in collusion with its appointees in the Election Commission, including Kumar.

Opposition parties say the voter deletions affected the outcome of some recent state elections won by the BJP, and have cast a shadow on the electoral process in the world's largest democracy.

Election Commission data, also cited by the BJP, shows about 130 million names, have been deleted from voter lists during the verification exercise, including 63 million who relocated, 30 million who could not be traced, and 28 million dead.

The commission says the count represents voter entries flagged during the draft revision stage, that the exercise is not complete yet, and voters wrongly removed can enrol again.

item.title: “We will ensure Gyanesh Kumar resigns”: Abhijeet Dipke says "ready to go to jail" ahead of march
item.description:
INDIA-POLITICS/GEN Z

Ahead of the ‘Jantar Mantar 2.0’ protest scheduled in New Delhi on Saturday, Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) activist Abhijeet Dipke, while departing from Mumbai to Delhi, said he was ready to go to jail and would continue his fight over the alleged deletion of votes, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Dipke said threats of imprisonment would not deter him from continuing the fight, adding that he was prepared to go to jail.

Speaking to ANI, Dipke said, " If you think you can stop us by threatening us with jail or trying to intimidate us with the fear of imprisonment, you are mistaken. We are ready to go to jail. If you want to imprison us, go ahead—impose the NSA, the UAPA, or whatever laws you wish—but we will continue to fight to save this country's democracy."

He claimed that people were being deprived of their voting rights, asserting that he would continue to fight to "save the democracy of India."

"And we will ensure Gyanesh Kumar resigns, because over 13 crore votes have been deleted and people are being stripped of their voting rights; we will keep fighting for that cause. We have to save the democracy of India," he further said.

Dipke also questioned the restrictions imposed in the national capital, alleging that the entire city had been shut down to protect Kumar.

"I fail to understand how Narendra Modi can shut down the entire national capital just to shield one man, Gyanesh Kumar. You have halted railway services, shut down the metro, blocked all roads, suspended the internet,” Dipke added.

Meanwhile, security arrangements have been stepped up across the national capital ahead of the proposed demonstration. More than 35,000 Delhi Police and paramilitary personnel have been deployed, amid heightened security measures and a directive from the Union Home Secretary to states and Union Territories to maintain law and order.

The demonstration, scheduled to be held at Jantar Mantar today, has been claimed to be aimed at seeking accountability over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. CJP has called for a large mobilisation despite the Delhi Police denying permission for the protest.

In an Instagram post, CJP said, "10th October. Jantar Mantar 2.0. We're coming together again to raise our voice against Gyanesh Kumar. Thousands of us are expected..."Following the announcement, Delhi Police instructed its teams to detain anyone attempting to stage a protest, irrespective of their location, according to the details provided. Police have also directed Central Armed Police Forces (CAPF) units not to issue weapons for deployment related to the demonstration. Letters have been sent to the concerned directorates regarding the allotment plan.

Unlike the arrangements made during the INDIA bloc protest, police teams have now been authorised to carry lathis and batons. In view of alleged attempts to record and circulate videos portraying police personnel in a negative light, teams have been instructed to avoid verbal confrontations with protesters.

Those detained are to be taken to six designated centres: Chhatrasal Stadium, Rajiv Gandhi Stadium, Yamuna Sports Complex, Surajmal Stadium, the Community Centre in Daulatpur and the Community Centre in Pandrawal.

Not just a naughty child
item.description:
Clinical practice can be challenging in Bangladesh, and more so if you are a psychiatrist. Your patient cries, shows anger and signs of distress.
And here you are, sitting with a curious face and non-judgmental attitude and trying to understand the explicit and implicit issues with the patient.
So, when a child of seven years entered my chamber, took two highlighters just to throw them away, jumped on the bed just to get down immediately, and ran amok, I was worried whether the child might get hurt.
I was curious, however, about the attitude of the parents. “Doctor, my child simply does not listen. He cannot sit still, does not concentrate on his studies, and is constantly getting complaints from school. He is just a naughty kid.”
For many parents and clinicians alike, this is a familiar story. A child who is constantly moving, interrupts others, forgets instructions, or struggles to complete schoolwork may quickly be labelled as “naughty,” “lazy,” “stubborn,” or “undisciplined.”
Parents fail to recognize it for what it is, and ultimately, children are subjected to repeated scolding or even physical punishment in an attempt to correct their behaviour.
But in some cases, these behaviours may reflect a neurodevelopmental condition known as attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD.
ADHD is not simply about being “too active.” It is a condition in which difficulties with attention, impulse control, and/or hyperactivity are persistent and developmentally inappropriate, and they interfere with everyday functioning.
At the same time, it is important to remember that not every active or inattentive child has ADHD. A child who occasionally loses concentration during homework does not necessarily have ADHD.
Children naturally have variations in attention, energy, and behaviour. However, when difficulties persist over time, occur in more than one setting such as home and school, and significantly interfere with learning, relationships or daily functioning, professional assessment may be warranted.
There is another important reason not to jump to conclusions. Sleep problems, anxiety, depression, learning difficulties, family stress, and excessive screen use can also affect a child's attention and behaviour. A proper assessment therefore requires more than simply checking a list of symptoms.
Calling a child “bad” or giving a “smack” does not teach self-control. It may instead damage the child's confidence and relationship with parents and teachers. Children with attention or behavioral difficulties often benefit more from clear expectations, predictable routines, positive reinforcement, and appropriately structured tasks.
For example, instead of yelling at a child, parents can set a specific and realistic goal: “For the next 15 minutes, let's complete these two pages.” Breaking larger tasks into smaller steps can make them easier to manage.
Schools also have an important role. Leadership, communication, discipline, and ultimately their world view is largely shaped by how they interact at school.
A child who repeatedly leaves his seat or fails to complete assignments should not automatically be treated as a disciplinary problem. Clear and brief instructions, reasonable breaks, structured classroom routines, and positive feedback may help such children participate more effectively.
A child’s problem must be communicated with their parents without labels; labelling will automatically make parents more frustrated in an already tiring battle.
Treatment is multi-faceted. Depending on the child's needs, it may involve behavioral interventions, parent-focused strategies, educational support and, when clinically appropriate, medication.
The goal is not simply to make a child “quiet.” The goal is to improve attention, self-regulation, learning, and overall functioning.
Most importantly, an ADHD diagnosis does not mean that a child's future is determined by the disorder. With appropriate assessment, support and treatment, children with ADHD can develop their abilities and lead productive and fulfilling lives.
So, the most important change we need is a change in the question we ask. Instead of asking, “Why is this child so naughty?” we should sometimes ask: “What is making this child struggle, and what kind of help does the child need?”
Understanding the reason behind a child's behavior may be the first step toward changing that child's future.
Dr Imdadul Magfur is a psychiatrist and psychotherapist, Sylhet MAG Osmani Medical College and Hospital.

item.title: From windows to waterfront: Manila Baywalk
item.description:
“If the story's any good, it's like Manila Hotel.”
One of the Philippines' most iconic properties—The Manila Hotel—proudly showcases this quote, attributed to master storyteller Ernest Hemingway about his famous stay in this grand old bayside hotel.
The legendary American author stayed there in February 1941, just months before the outbreak of World War II in the Pacific. During Hemingway’s time at the luxury bayside property, he famously mingled with local journalists at the bar and addressed the Philippine Writers League.
This image, again taken from inside a room of The Manila Hotel captures the inner harbor slip and the hotel’s pool area directly underneath. The vibrant, colorful structures situated across the water on the left side belong to the Museo Pambata, an interactive children’s museum situated right along Roxas Boulevard. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
Seventy-eight years after the author of The Old Man and the Sea walked these halls, I stepped inside a beautifully decorated bay-view room of the historic hotel. It was the dry season of 2019, a period prolonged by an El Niño event.
I was on a business trip, remaining busy for most of April 2019 while engaging with farming communities and policy planners from across Asia. Whenever I caught a break between meetings and workshops, I retreated to the relaxation of my room, spending time standing by the windows overlooking Manila Bay, its harbors, piers, and walkways.
This photo was taken from The Manila Hotel, looking out over Manila Bay toward the Manila Ocean theme park and its adjoining pier. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
Peeking through the glass, the bay felt tantalizingly close, yet a packed business schedule ultimately prevented me from taking a stroll along the Manila Baywalk. This was not the first time my trips to Metro Manila had taken me to various parts of the Philippines while leaving Manila Bay just out of reach.
During one of my earliest visits to Manila over three decades ago, I remember having to detour while traveling between cities within the greater metropolitan area due to the city’s rapid expansion through land reclamation. I witnessed firsthand how Filipinos were reclaiming land from Manila Bay—a massive natural harbor connected directly to the South China Sea. In fact, much of the waterfront along Metro Manila is built on reclaimed land, which today includes vital institutions like the Senate of the Philippines and the SM Mall of Asia, arguably the largest mall in the region.
The writer standing along the Manila Baywalk at night, with the illuminated high-rise skyline of the Malate district in Metro Manila, Philippines, serving as the background. Docked in the calm waters behind him are several boats and yachts moored near the historic Manila Yacht Club. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
I managed a brief glimpse of Manila Bay during a past trip to Pasay City, when I walked through the sprawling corners of the Mall of Asia. Pasay is deeply tied to the land reclamation history of the area; the entire mall complex sits on reclaimed land situated directly along the waterfront. However, pressed by other urgent preoccupations on that visit, I only managed a quick round of shopping and a brief stroll across the road, unable to spend any real time by the bayside.
In more recent years, I returned to Manila in 2022, but once again, the bay area eluded me.
Then came the end of the wet season the following year. In October 2023, I found myself attending business meetings and staying for a few days at the Century Park Hotel in Manila’s Malate district. This time, I finally made it to Manila Bay, spending a long-awaited evening by the Baywalk promenade.
This specific overhead vantage point is captured from one of the harbor-view rooms inside the historic The Manila Hotel, which overlooks the port complex and the outdoor swimming pools visible at the bottom edge. The primary white buildings situated along the Pier 15 at the Manila South Harbour compose the Eva Macapagal Super Terminal that functions as a central passenger hub for ferries and cruise ships. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
Malate’s name carries its own coastal history. Tagalog is spoken by many Filipinos, and its standardized form, Filipino, is the national language. The name "Malate" is a corruption of the word maalat (meaning saline) in Tagalog, which refers to the brackish waters where the river estuary—today’s Estero de Malate—meets Manila Bay. True to the literal meaning of the district, I found that the bay was actually not far from my hotel.
After wrapping up a day of business, I stepped out of the Century Park Hotel one evening and walked about a kilometer until I reached the wide Roxas Boulevard. That arterial waterfront road and promenade led me straight to the shores of Manila Bay.
As I stood along the Manila Baywalk at night, I watched several boats and yachts moored near the historic Manila Yacht Club. From that vantage point, the illuminated, high-rise skyline of the Malate district looked beautiful.
The Baywalk stretches for about two kilometers, serving as a popular seaside promenade and beachfront that offers visitors a space for quality leisure, flanked by nearby eateries and rooftop bars. Many admire the area most for providing the best vantage points to view the iconic, golden Manila Bay sunset.
The writer having a tête-à-tête at The Manila Hotel lobby with Edith Burgos, a highly prominent human rights advocate globally recognized for her decades of leadership in International Coalition Against Enforced Disappearances (ICAED). Photo: Dhaka Tribune
A quick flip through the pages of military history generates even deeper interest in the area, as Manila Bay has borne witness to many conflicts. The bay was the setting for the Battle of Manila Bay in 1898, where American troops led by Commodore George Dewey seized the area in a definitive showcase of United States naval strength, destroying or capturing all major Spanish ships. With its proud historic past and abundant marine life, Manila Bay became the ocean portal and epicenter for Philippine governance, economy, and industry.
The bay also hosted unexpected visitors. In 1905, during the Russo-Japanese War, three surviving Russian protected cruisers—the Aurora , Oleg , and Zhemchug —managed to make port in US-controlled Manila for repairs following the Battle of Tsushima. Because the United States was neutral in the conflict, the trio of warships and their crews remained interned in the bay until the war officially ended that September.
Decades later, during World War II, Corregidor Island in Manila Bay was captured by Japanese forces. Much earlier, various other historic battles were fought from this naval base, including the Battles of La Naval de Manila in 1646, which finally ended Dutch attempts to seize the Philippines.
The foundation cornerstone tablet of The Manila Hotel is preserved on display near the main building’s entrance and veranda grounds, honoring the structure’s century-old heritage. This plaque commemorates September 1st, 1910, the exact date when the United States Secretary of War, Jacob M. Dickinson, laid the cornerstone for the iconic hotel during his official visit to the Philippine Islands. Designed by New York architect William E. Parsons as part of Daniel Burnham’s urban master plan for Manila, the hotel officially opened two years later on July 4, 1912. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
The night walk along the Manila Baywalk remains fresh in my memory, a vivid highlight of a relatively recent visit. Though I missed the world-famous Manila Bay sunset on that particular evening, walking the promenade after dark offered its own distinct, physical magic. As night fell, a steady, warm maritime breeze swept in from the bay, providing a welcome relief from the city’s dense heat. With the deepening darkness, the cityscape truly came alive.
Towering hotels, bustling restaurants, and historical buildings along Roxas Boulevard lit up, casting a neon glow that danced across the pavement and the water's surface. Standing there, I was enveloped by a unique urban symphony: the rhythmic lapping of waves against the seawall blending seamlessly with the distant hum of rushing traffic and the faint, soulful strumming of a street musician’s guitar.
The writer takes a selfie inside the grand Lobby Lounge of The Manila Hotel, showcasing its iconic Filipino-colonial architecture. The backdrop highlights the hotel’s signature handcrafted crystal and capiz-shell chandeliers, white arches, dark wood-panel ceilings, and distinctive carved wooden screens behind the reception desks. This space has historically welcomed heads of state, celebrities, and literary icons since its opening in 1912. Photo: Dhaka Tribune

item.title: Dhaka’s air quality 4th worst in the world Saturday morning
item.description:
Dhaka, the overcrowded capital city of Bangladesh, has ranked 4th on the list of cities with the worst air quality, with an AQI index of 181 at 9:06am on Saturday.
Dhaka’s air was classified as "unhealthy", according to the air quality and pollution city ranking.
Singapore, Malaysia’s Kuala Lumpur and India's Kolkata occupied the first, second and third spots in the list, with AQI scores of 200, 198 and 192, respectively.
When the AQI value for particle pollution is between 101 and 150, air quality is considered "unhealthy for sensitive groups", between 150 and 200 is "unhealthy", between 201 and 300 is said to be "very unhealthy", while a reading of 301+ is considered "hazardous", posing serious health risks to residents.
The AQI, an index for reporting daily air quality, informs people how clean or polluted the air of a certain city is and what associated health effects might be a concern for them.
The AQI in Bangladesh is based on five pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), NO2, CO, SO2, and ozone.
Dhaka has long been grappling with air pollution issues. Its air quality usually turns unhealthy in winter and improves during the monsoon.

item.title: Police Additional DIG Tutul Chakraborty dismissed from service
item.description:
The government has dismissed Additional Deputy Inspector General (DIG) of Police Tutul Chakraborty from service after finding him guilty of misconduct, including leaving his post ahead of schedule and using an airport VIP lounge while identifying himself as a “DIG.”
The decision was announced in a notification issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs on Wednesday. According to the notification, Chakraborty was attached to the office of the Rajshahi Range DIG while under suspension and had been “absconding” since January 23.
The notification said Chakraborty had been granted 2 days of leave with permission on November 14 and 15, 2025, followed by 3 days of casual leave from November 16 to 18. However, on November 13, the day before his leave began, he left his post ahead of schedule without submitting the required departure report.
On that day, Chakraborty concealed his identity and introduced himself as a DIG. He then used the DIG lounge and boarded a US-Bangla Airlines flight from Shah Makhdum Airport in Rajshahi to Dhaka at around 10:20am.
The notification further stated that he had used the VIP lounge at Rajshahi Airport several times before, identifying himself as “DIG, Rajshahi Range.” The matter came to the attention of various intelligence agencies, and the notification said his actions had severely damaged the police's image in the eyes of the public.
According to the Ministry of Home Affairs, these actions amounted to gross negligence in performing public duties, disregard for lawful orders and conduct contrary to departmental discipline. Under the Government Employees (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 2018, the actions constituted “misconduct,” a punishable offense.
A departmental case was filed against Chakraborty over the allegations. On February 5 this year, he was issued a show-cause notice along with a statement of allegations and a charge sheet. However, he did not submit a written reply within the stipulated time or apply for an extension.
The notification said an investigating officer was appointed on April 2 to examine the allegations. Following the investigation, a report was submitted on May 7, concluding that the misconduct charges against Chakraborty had been proven beyond doubt.
Based on the investigation report, a second show-cause notice was issued on June 16, asking why he should not be dismissed from service. He did not respond to that notice either.
The government subsequently reviewed the allegations, the investigation report and other documents before making a preliminary decision to dismiss Chakraborty from service.
The government then sought the opinion of the Bangladesh Public Service Commission, which recommended dismissal on September 14.
The matter was subsequently sent to the president for approval. On October 5, the president approved the dismissal proposal.
Accordingly, Chakraborty has been given the major penalty of dismissal from service under the relevant provisions of the Government Employees (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 2018.

item.title: Faqir Mahbub calls for global cooperation to ensure children’s online safety
item.description:
Minister of the Ministries for Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology, and Science and Technology Faqir Mahbub Anam has called for stronger global cooperation, joint initiatives among stakeholders and the exchange of international best practices to ensure children's safety in the digital environment.
He made the call while delivering Bangladesh's statement at the Business IT Breakfast titled "Digital Childhood Without Borders: Best International Practices for Child Safety Online", held in Moscow, Russia, on Thursday.
Representing Bangladesh at the event, the minister also conveyed, on behalf of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, his appreciation to the Global Digital Forum and the Alliance for the Protection of Children in the Digital Environment for undertaking this timely initiative.
Faqir Mahbub said Bangladesh is undergoing rapid digital transformation, enabling children to benefit from the online world for education and personal development.
At the same time, however, they are increasingly exposed to new and evolving forms of online risks, he added.
Ensuring children's digital safety is no longer the sole responsibility of parents or teachers; rather, it is a shared responsibility involving all stakeholders, including governments, online platforms, technology companies and civil society.
He said that under the leadership of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, Bangladesh is working to strengthen relevant digital protection laws and legal frameworks, including the Cyber Security Act, to protect children's data and prevent online exploitation.
The minister, however, noted that such challenges cannot be addressed through legislation alone. In this regard, sharing international experiences, best practices and effective solutions that can be implemented on a broad scale is critically important, he said.
Referring to the review of the draft Joint Statement and Terms of Reference of the proposed Global Alliance to Protect Children in the Digital Environment, the minister congratulated the Russian Federation on taking this important initiative.
He further said the proposed document presents a comprehensive, child-rights-based framework in line with the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child.
The minister expressed Bangladesh's strong support for the three core principles of the proposed initiative, saying that the best interests of the child must be given the highest priority, the shared responsibility of all stakeholders must be ensured, and experiences and best practices must be exchanged through international cooperation.
He emphasized the importance of establishing a multilateral stakeholder framework that ensures equitable representation of different geographical regions, including the Asia-Pacific region.
Such a framework would provide opportunities for the realities, challenges and experiences of developing countries like Bangladesh to be appropriately reflected in the formulation of global strategies.
At the same time, Bangladesh welcomes the proposal to establish a Digital Childhood Safety Index and a dedicated platform for research and the exchange of best practices.
Faqir Mahbub Anam said enhancing digital literacy among children, parents and teachers is also a crucial foundation of the initiative.
He observed that developing the necessary knowledge and awareness in line with the rapid advancement of technologies, including artificial intelligence, could help establish an effective preventive mechanism against online harms.
He said Bangladesh remains firmly committed to the principles outlined in the Joint Statement of the Global Alliance to Protect Children in the Digital Environment.
Bangladesh is keen to work closely with the Alliance to protect children from online bullying, sexual harassment, data theft and other forms of digital harm.
The Alliance can play an important role in building a bridge between national policies and global cooperation, he added.
The telecommunications minister said Bangladesh is ready to work with all relevant stakeholders to build a future in which every child, regardless of nationality, can explore the digital world safely, creatively and without fear.
He said the collective initiative was an investment in future generations and that the digital future being built must be not only connected but also safe, inclusive and child-friendly.
Representatives from more than 100 countries participated in the international forum.

item.title: UK parliamentary delegation meets political and civil society leaders
item.description:
The British All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) on Bangladesh has held a series of high-level meetings with political and civil society leaders during its visit to Bangladesh this week.
The delegation began its engagements on Tuesday with a meeting with British High Commissioner to Bangladesh Sarah Cooke. It subsequently met Deputy Speaker Barrister Kayser Kamal MP at the Bangladesh Parliament and held meetings at ministerial offices with Minister Humaiun Kobir, Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury MP and Adviser Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir.
On Wednesday, the delegation visited United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) sites in Cox’s Bazar and paid a courtesy call to the offices of the Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commissioner (RRRC) to gain first-hand insight into the humanitarian and refugee crisis affecting more than 1 million Rohingya in Bangladesh.
On Thursday, the delegation met President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir at Bangabhaban. Discussions covered women's representation in Parliament, the July Charter and constitutional change, political party reform, training and development for parliamentarians, and truth and reconciliation processes for historical rights abuses.
The delegation also met Minister for Cultural Affairs Nitin Roy Chowdhury MP and Nipun Roy Chowdhury MP at the minister's offices.
Further meetings have been held with opposition leaders and civil society figures.
The delegation also visited the offices of BRAC and the BRAC Institute for Governance and Development, as well as the Drik Picture Library. At Drik, it convened a meeting with leading representatives of Bangladeshi civil society organizations, focusing primarily on women's, minority and indigenous rights.
The delegation's visit will continue with further engagements over the coming days.
The delegation is supported by the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association UK (CPA UK).

item.title: "Why are people's voices being suppressed?": Bollywood actor Imran Khan detained in Mumbai
item.description:
Bollywood actor Imran Khan was detained by the Mumbai Police on Saturday at August Kranti Maidan in Mumbai, the proposed venue for a protest in support of CJP’s protest call.

Following his detention, the actor shared a picture of himself apparently seated inside a police van. He accompanied the photograph with a light-hearted caption, writing, “Apparently I’m going for a drive.”

Speaking to the media, Imran Khan clarified that he was not present with any specific demands but had come forward in his capacity as a citizen of Mumbai. He said he wanted to understand why freedom of movement was being restricted and why people’s voices were being suppressed.

Mamata, Kejriwal and Dipke among hundreds detained, Delhi locked down to foil protest

“I don't have demands. I am here as a citizen, as a person who lives in this city. I am here to see why freedom of movement is being restricted. Why are people's voices being suppressed? That is why I am here,” the actor said.

He further stated that he was not affiliated with any organisation and was participating in an individual capacity.

Emphasising his position, Imran added, “I don't have any right to demand anything from people. I am not a part of any organisation. I will stand as a representative.”

Dhruv Rathee arrested over Jantar Mantar protest

The actor’s detention comes amid police action at August Kranti Maidan, where authorities have detained more than 400 people, according to the Mumbai Police.

On the other hand, around 1,000 protesters have been detained across the national capital so far while attempting to march towards Jantar Mantar for a Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led protest demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, Delhi Police sources said on Saturday.

item.title: Afghanistan fight back through Rahmat, trail Bangladesh by 135 runs
item.description:
Afghanistan ended the second day of the Test against Bangladesh at 211 for four, trailing by 135 runs in the first innings with six wickets remaining.

Rahmat Shah remained unbeaten on 84, while Ikram Alikhil was not out on 24. The pair put together an unbroken 72-run partnership for the fifth wicket off 194 balls to steady Afghanistan after Bangladesh made inroads into their batting line-up.

Rahmat, who has struck his way to within 16 runs of a century, and Ikram ensured Afghanistan did not lose another wicket before stumps.

Bangladesh had started the day with two wickets remaining and added 29 runs in 8.3 overs before being bowled out for 346. After completing their innings, the Bangladeshi bowlers spent much of the day waiting for breakthroughs.

Their quickest pair of wickets came just five balls apart, but Bangladesh were unable to maintain that momentum towards the end of the day as Rahmat and Ikram dug in.

Abdul Malik also made a valuable contribution, scoring 62 before being dismissed. Ebadot Hossain took two wickets for Bangladesh, while Hasan Mahmud and Mehidy Hasan Miraz claimed one each.

Bangladesh had earlier posted 346 in their first innings, with Tanzid Hasan scoring 83 and Shadman Islam making 67. Naeem Hasan remained unbeaten on 35.

For Afghanistan, Saleem took four wickets for 82 runs, while Yamin claimed three for 79.

Afghanistan will resume on the third day with Rahmat Shah approaching his century and the side looking to cut the deficit before Bangladesh can take control of the match.

Bangladesh 1st innings: 346 all out in 92.3 overs (Tanzid Hasan 83, Shadman Islam 67, Naeem Hasan 35*; Saleem 4/82, Yamin 3/79).

Afghanistan 1st innings: 211/4 in 79 overs (Rahmat Shah 84*, Abdul Malik 62, Ikram Alikhil 24*; Ebadot Hossain 2/50, Hasan Mahmud 1/36, Mehidy Hasan Miraz 1/36).

item.title: Police officers in Khulna asked not to travel alone at night
item.description:
Police in Khulna district have been instructed not to travel alone at night after a police inspector was seriously injured in a knife attack by muggers in Khulna city.

The directive was issued in an official letter signed by the superintendent of police of the District Special Branch (DSB) on Friday night.

The letter said special operations were under way in Rupsa, Terokhada, Dighalia and Batiaghata police station areas in response to the prevailing law and order situation and several recent incidents. It also noted recent attacks by criminals on law enforcement personnel.

In view of the overall situation, police personnel engaged in special operations and other duties were instructed not to travel alone at night to ensure their personal safety. Unit in-charges were asked to take the necessary measures.

Copies of the letter were sent to all relevant offices and police stations under the district police.

Khulna Superintendent of Police Sarker Omar Faruk told Prothom Alo that a police inspector was seriously injured in a knife attack by muggers while returning after conducting a special operation in Rupsa police station area late on Thursday night. The inspector was returning home by rickshaw after crossing the river by ferry.

He was carrying two mobile phones and a wallet when he was attacked by muggers in front of Khulna Collegiate Girls' School. He may have tried to resist the attackers at the time. He was in plain clothes.

The inspector was sent to Dhaka in critical condition and is still receiving treatment at a private hospital there.

The superintendent of police said the restriction on travelling alone at night was imposed after the incident, keeping the safety of every member of the district police in mind.

The precaution was intended to prevent police personnel from falling victim to muggers while returning home after duty, he added.

Asked whether the directive could convey a message that the police were feeling insecure, Sarker Omar Faruk said, “Actually, this is an internal letter. We cannot include all the details in a letter. The main purpose is to ensure that no police personnel fall victim to muggers.”

Police Inspector Shah Alam, 43, was attacked by muggers in front of Khulna Collegiate School on Khan Jahan Ali Road in Khulna city at around 2:30am on Friday.

According to police sources, he was travelling by rickshaw towards the city after conducting a special operation in Rupsa upazila when three muggers intercepted him in front of the school and snatched his money and mobile phone. When he resisted, the attackers struck both his wrists with a sharp machete.

Police later rescued him and took him to hospital. As his condition deteriorated, he was transferred to Dhaka for better treatment.

Khulna district police launched a special operation on Tuesday night to arrest criminals and recover illegal firearms.

The operation began following the shooting death of Akhtar Dhali, whose son Joy Dhali had been murdered about a month and a half earlier, in Rupsa on Monday. Another man was also shot dead at a tea stall in the Formayshkhana area of Dighalia on the same day.

item.title: Crowne Plaza Dhaka Gulshan transforms giving into meaningful action
item.description:
Crowne Plaza Dhaka Gulshan turned IHG Hotels & Resorts’ Giving for Good Month 2026 into a month of action, bringing together colleagues, entrepreneurs, partners, guests and members of the community around one shared purpose - giving back, reports a press release.

As part of IHG’s Journey to tomorrow, the hotel transformed September into a series of initiatives where giving took many forms - from donating blood and supporting women-led businesses to running for charity and making personal contributions.

Starting with a drop of hope

The journey began with “Drops of Hope,” a blood donation camp organised in collaboration with the Bangladesh Thalassemia Foundation.

Nearly 50 per cent of the hotel’s employees came forward to donate blood, with the potential to support 60–70 thalassemia patients and their families who depend on regular transfusions.

30 Women. 30 Stories. One Purpose.

The second edition of W.O.W Market - Women of Worth and Wonder brought together 30 women-led businesses, giving entrepreneurs, artisans and creators a platform to showcase and sell their products.

From handwoven clothing and handmade products to jute and coconut-husk crafts and homemade food, the market celebrated local creativity while creating direct social impact.

Each participating entrepreneur contributed Tk 3,000 towards their stall, with the full amount donated to Mojar School, while all sales went directly to the participating businesses.

A step towards giving back to the community

The giving continued with Run for Charity: Meaningful Marathon 2.0, bringing together 200+ runners - including colleagues, corporate partners, community members, running enthusiasts and former Bangladesh national footballer Zahid Hasan Ameli.

Participants contributed Tk 1,500 each, generating more than Tk 300,000 towards the hotel’s Giving for Good fundraising effort in support of Mojar School.

What began as a 5-kilometre run became a shared expression of community, fitness and purpose.

From many contributions to one collective gift

The journey culminated in the Joy of Giving Charity Dinner on 1 October, where colleagues, guests, partners and supporters came together to celebrate the spirit of giving.

Hotel colleagues made personal contributions of Tk 1.5 lacs, and through the collective Giving for Good initiatives, a total of Tk 12 lacs was raised for Mojar School.

The Tk12 lacs cheque was formally handed over to Mojar School by Firoze Asad, senior group advisor & member of the board, Doreen, together with Karthi VK, general manager, Crowne Plaza Dhaka Gulshan. The contribution will support 200+ underprivileged children, helping provide education, nutrition and essential support.

A shared commitment to giving

Firoze Asad, senior group advisor & member of the Board, Doreen said,

“What makes me particularly happy is that this has not been just one event. The team has created a meaningful journey of giving - Drops of Hope, the WOW Market, the Meaningful Charity Run, and now the Joy of Giving Dinner.”

He also recognised the work of Arian Arif, founder of Mojar School, and the organisation’s efforts to provide children not only with shelter and care, but more importantly, education and an opportunity for a better future.

Karthi VK, general manager, Crowne Plaza Dhaka Gulshan, said, “Giving for Good becomes truly meaningful when it moves beyond a campaign and becomes a shared commitment. This month, our colleagues, partners, entrepreneurs, runners, guests and community members all found different ways to give back.”

An evening of giving and celebration

The Joy of Giving Dinner also featured an evening of entertainment, with magician Saqlain Hossain captivating guests with his magic, followed by a comedy performance. Students from Mojar School presented a special cultural performance, adding a meaningful touch to the celebration.

The programme concluded with a vote of thanks, followed by music entertainment and a lavish buffet dinner.

Through Giving for Good, Crowne Plaza Dhaka Gulshan demonstrated how small acts of giving can come together to create a collective impact - helping build opportunities for children to learn, grow and dream of a brighter future.

item.title: Driver lured schoolgirl with promise of a shortcut, then raped and killed her: Police
item.description:
The Class-VII student (15) whose body was recovered from a paddy field in Cumilla, had taken a CNG-run auto-rickshaw at Paduar Bazar Bishwa Road to return home, police said.

The driver Sumon Mia (35) took her to an isolated area, claiming that he was taking a shortcut. He then raped and killed her.

Sumon Mia has been arrested in connection with the case, according to Police.

Police said their preliminary investigation indicated that Sumon was solely involved in the rape and murder. During interrogation, Sumon confessed to his involvement in the killing.

An iPhone used by the girl was also recovered based on information he provided.

Pankaj Barua, Additional Superintendent of Police (Crime), disclosed this information at a press conference at the district police office on Saturday. Mizanur Rahman, officer-in-charge (OC) of Lalmai Police Station and officials from the district police and Detective Branch (DB) were also present.

Sumon was detained in Chattogram on Friday. After the incident, he fled and went into hiding at his brother’s place, police said.

Sumon used to drive a CNG-run auto-rickshaw on a rental basis. His home is in Kachua upazila of Chandpur. However, as he had no land or house of his own there, he lived at his in-laws’ home in Lalmai upazila. He mostly carried passengers at night in Paduar Bazar and nearby areas.

Auto-rickshaw stopped in an isolated, dark place

At the press conference, police said the girl got off a bus in the Paduar Bazar Bishwa Road area on the night of 8 October. She then went to look for an auto-rickshaw in front of the Tisha bus counter to return home. At one point, she agreed to pay Tk 300 and got into Sumon’s CNG-run auto-rickshaw.

After travelling a short distance, the girl gave the driver Tk 100. Sumon used the money to buy bananas and bread. He then offered to take her to her destination by a shortcut. The auto-rickshaw proceeded towards Lalmai via Bijra Bazar along the Cumilla-Chandpur road. The driver stopped the vehicle at an isolated, dark spot.

According to police, Sumon attempted to rape the girl. When she screamed, he wrapped a gamchha around her neck. He then took her to a paddy field, where he raped and killed her.

iPhone left in bushes after bathing in a pond

Police claimed that, fearing for her life on the night of the incident, the girl sent her live location to her father’s mobile phone and pleaded for help. Her father did not see the message at the time. He saw it early in the morning and later went to the location, where he found police recovering his daughter’s body.

Additional Superintendent of Police Pankaj Barua said at the press conference that Sumon left the auto-rickshaw at the scene after killing the girl.

He later took a bath in a pond, left the girl’s iPhone in a wooded area and travelled to Chattogram.

The girl’s body was recovered on Thursday morning beside the embankment of a paddy field in Lalmai upazila.

item.title: Afghanistan reach 131-2 at tea against Bangladesh
item.description:
Afghanistan reached 131 for two at tea on the second day of the Test against Bangladesh, scoring 97 runs in the second session to reduce their deficit to 215 runs.

Abdul Malik was unbeaten on 60, his maiden half-century in Test cricket, while Rahmat Shah was batting on 33. The pair added an unbroken 67 runs for the third wicket after Afghanistan lost two early wickets.

Hasan Mahmud and Ebadot Hossain took a wicket each for Bangladesh, but the hosts' three spinners — Mehidy Hasan Miraz, Taijul Islam and Naeem Hasan — were yet to make a breakthrough.

Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto turned to Hasan again in search of a wicket as Malik and Rahmat continued to build their partnership on a pitch offering little assistance to the spinners.

Bangladesh had made a promising start to the day with the ball. Hasan dismissed opener Sediqullah Atal for 17, with Tanzid Hasan taking a catch at slip. Atal had earlier survived a strong appeal for a possible edge behind, as the umpire turned down the appeal and Bangladesh opted against a review. Replays later showed a clear spike on UltraEdge, suggesting Bangladesh had missed an opportunity to dismiss him earlier.

Ebadot broke the second partnership when he dismissed Shahidullah for 20. Shahidullah attempted to pull a short delivery but edged the ball towards deep fine leg, where Hasan Mahmud ran forward and dived to complete an excellent catch. Ebadot celebrated the wicket with his trademark salute.

Afghanistan ended the first session at 34 for one after scoring 63 runs and losing three wickets across 21.2 overs in the session, including the end of Bangladesh's innings.

Bangladesh resumed the day at 317 for eight and added 29 runs before being bowled out for 346. Naeem Hasan remained unbeaten on 35, helping the hosts extend their total.

Bangladesh had been well placed at 221 for two at one stage but lost their final eight wickets for 125 runs. Afghanistan's Saleem took four wickets.

Bangladesh's first-innings total was below the ground's average first-innings score of 360, leaving Afghanistan with an opportunity to build a substantial response. At tea, however, they still trailed by 215 runs, with eight wickets remaining.

item.title: Mamata, Kejriwal and Dipke among hundreds detained, Delhi locked down to foil protest
item.description:
INDIA-POLITICS/GEN Z

Police detained hundreds of protesters and the "Cockroach" youth movement founder in Delhi on Saturday as security forces locked down parts of the capital to thwart a demonstration demanding the resignation of India's election chief.

Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed across the city, mobile internet services were suspended in the central business district and dozens of metro stations and markets were shut as authorities moved to stop a rally organised by the Cockroach movement.

The protest was aimed at Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a revision of voter lists that critics say disproportionately benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

The movement had planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site in central Delhi. But the area was sealed off by security forces before the demonstration began.

However, small protests broke out elsewhere in the city, including at a popular crafts market and the memorial to freedom movement leader Mahatma Gandhi, with protesters shouting slogans demanding Kumar's resignation.

"Long live the revolution," some young protesters chanted in central Delhi as police chased them and dragged scores of others into buses to be taken away, even as more arrived, a Reuters witness said.

"This is violating the rights of the people and the country will not tolerate this anymore," Yogendra Solanki told Reuters as police escorted him away.

Police also detained Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke and senior leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka when their flight from Mumbai landed in Delhi, the group said in a statement.

Delhi locked down to foil protest

Television footage showed Dipke challenging officers who approached him on board the aircraft.

"I have come to be arrested, arrest me ... I am not afraid of you guys," he said.

"No, this is not an arrest," one officer replied. "Please cooperate."

The movement condemned what it called the "authoritarian detention" of its leaders, demanded their immediate release and said the protest would continue regardless.

Some opposition lawmakers and former chief ministers Mamata Banerjee of West Bengal and Arvind Kejriwal of Delhi were also detained, TV channels showed.

Representatives of two digital news outlets said police briefly detained four of their reporters while they were covering the demonstrations. A Reuters journalist was also detained briefly before being released.

Some lawyers protesting outside the Supreme Court were also picked up and later freed, according to the president of the court's bar association.
There was no immediate comment from police on the detentions.

Across the sprawling capital of about 20 million people, security forces mounted checkpoints on major roads and at city entry points. Police officers boarded buses searching for protesters, while vehicles were subjected to inspections.

Barricades and concrete blocks stopped traffic, while anti-riot vehicles mounted with tear gas guns were stationed on key routes.

New challange to Modi

The demonstrations represent one of the most serious tests yet for Modi, stemming from allegations that election authorities improperly revised voter rolls ahead of recent state polls.

Protests have gathered momentum since last week, when the Indian Express newspaper reported that two election commissioners had questioned and disagreed with Kumar over revisions that removed roughly 130 million names from voter lists.

Kumar has not commented but the Election Commission and the BJP have denied allegations of wrongdoing.

The BJP says its electoral success reflects Modi's popularity and India's economic growth, and accuses opposition parties of spreading misinformation because they have failed to win elections.

Nonetheless, the near daily protests pose a new challenge for Modi, just months after demonstrations over exam paper leaks forced his education minister to quit.

The unrest also comes ahead of a series of important state elections beginning in early 2027.

Saturday's restrictions showed Modi's government had "officially waged war against its own people", KC Venugopal, a senior leader of the main opposition Congress party said.

BJP spokesperson Sambit Patra said democracy had prevailed over mob rule.

Deletions affected state polls, opposition alleges

Opposition parties say the voter deletions affected the outcome of some recent state elections won by the BJP, and have cast a shadow on elections in the world's largest democracy.

Election Commission data show about 130 million voter entries were removed during the verification exercise, including 63 million people who had relocated, 30 million who could not be traced and 28 million who had died.

The commission says the removals relate to entries identified during the draft revision process and that any eligible voter incorrectly deleted can re-enrol.
